title: The camel's choice
hookLine: every family wants him as guest, and he lets the camel choose, and it kneels near Abu Ayyub's house (sirah)

cards: Who gets the guest? That's the question in the streets of Yathrib as the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, rides in. The city has invited him, and household after household wants him under its own roof.
In Ibn Ishaq's sirah, one clan after another steps out and takes hold of the camel's rein: stay with us, we have numbers, we have strength, we will protect you.
Any answer he gives will honor one family and pass over the rest, on his very first day. Today: the camel's choice.

teach.h: LET HER GO, SHE IS UNDER COMMAND.
teach.b: His answer, as Ibn Ishaq tells it, is gentle and simple. Let her go her way, he says of the camel, for she is under command. So the rein is let go, and the camel walks on through the town with everyone watching.
Bukhari picks up the scene from there.
The camel kneels at an open place where dates were spread out to dry, belonging to two orphan boys. And the Prophet says: this, if Allah wills, is the place to stay. Then he does something careful.
He calls the two boys and asks to buy the land for a mosque. They say, in effect: no, we'll give it to you.
He refuses the gift and pays for it. On that ground the mosque of Medina is built, and in the meantime he lodges nearby, in the house of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.

Muslim's collection keeps a small scene from those days: Abu Ayyub, living upstairs, can't bear to walk above the Prophet's head, and asks him to move to the upper floor. Consider what the camel spared everyone.
No clan could say: he chose them over us.

The choice was left to the camel, which, in his words, was under command, and he passed over no family himself. And once the place was found, he didn't just take it. He paid two orphans what it was worth.
Letting go of choosing didn't mean letting go of care.

how: Muslims retell the camel's kneeling from the sirah and Sahih al-Bukhari when speaking of the founding of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, and honor Abu Ayyub al-Ansari as his host.

o: the man who took him into his home in Medina
the clan leader who held the camel's rein
an orphan who owned the date-drying ground

games.q: the camel's choice — tap the pairs.
p: took hold of the camel's rein
knelt at a place for drying dates
offered the land as a gift

s: the Prophet chose the strongest clan to stay with
he let the camel walk free, so no clan was chosen over another.
he accepted the orphans' land as a gift
he refused the gift and paid for it.
the mosque of Medina was built where the camel knelt
Bukhari places it on the land of the two orphans.

games.q: you've arrived in a new city. every family is pulling your camel's rein, begging you to stay with them. what do you do?
o: stay with the most powerful clan.
let the camel walk, and stay where she kneels.
stay one night with each family in turn.
games.why: in Ibn Ishaq he says let her go, she is under command; Bukhari says she knelt on the orphans' land, and he bought it for the mosque.

practice: Think of a small decision on your plate today where several good options are tugging at you and it doesn't much matter which one wins: where to eat, which task to start.
Notice your hands on the rein, then loosen them, and let something else choose, the nearest one, or the one someone else prefers. If you pray, you can hand the choice to Allah.

wordCard.voice: Abu Ayyub. In whose house the Prophet lodged near the spot where the camel, under command, chose to kneel. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'under command', what the sirah has him say of the camel.

carryVoice: Your line: let the camel choose. No family passed over, and two orphans paid in full. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the clans take the rein; 'let her go her way, for she is under command')
Sahih al-Bukhari 3906 (the camel kneels at the drying place of two orphans; 'this, if Allah wills, is the place'; he buys the land)
Sahih Muslim 2053 (Abu Ayyub's house; the upper floor)
